content.title: About
content.content: Asparagus is the young shoot of the herbaceous plant Asparagus officinalis, cultivated in temperate regions. Fresh asparagus has a delicate, slightly nutty flavor and a crisp texture. Cooking it with a small amount of oil enhances its aroma and makes its nutrients more bioavailable.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Asparagus is one of the oldest cultivated vegetables, grown for over 2,000 years.
In ancient Rome, asparagus was considered a delicacy reserved for the elite.
There are three main varieties: green, white (grown in darkness), and purple.
The harvest season in the Northern Hemisphere typically runs from April to June.
Light sautéing in oil brings out aromatic compounds that are otherwise muted.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Asparagus provides folate (B9), vitamin B6, and thiamine, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Low‑calorie fiber source
items.content: One cup of cooked asparagus delivers about 2 g of dietary fiber, aiding digestion and satiety.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: It contains glutathione, vitamin C, and vitamin E, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Heart‑supporting nutrients
items.content: Potassium and folate help maintain normal blood pressure, while plant compounds may improve lipid profiles.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: Asparagus supplies iron, magnesium, and zinc, essential for blood formation and immune health.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to asparagus, such as skin rash or swelling.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Asparagus contains oxalates, which in excess can contribute to kidney stone formation.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: For sensitive people, large portions may cause gas and abdominal discomfort.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Quickly sauté asparagus in olive or sunflower oil, add it to salads, soups, or pasta. Before cooking, trim the tough outer part of the stalk. Lightly browned asparagus retains its crunch and aroma while improving absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh asparagus in the refrigerator wrapped in a slightly damp towel and placed in a plastic bag; use within 3–5 days. Cooked asparagus should be kept in an airtight container in the fridge and consumed within 2 days.

bread-wheat-or-cracked-wheat-made-from-h.title: Bread, wheat or cracked wheat, homemade or bakery, toasted

content.title: About
content.content: Bread made from whole wheat or cracked wheat is a whole‑grain product created from intact wheat kernels that are coarsely milled and baked into slices. It can be prepared at home or bought from a bakery and then toasted to develop a crunchy crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The traditional method of making whole‑grain wheat bread dates back thousands of years.
Toasting intensifies aroma and creates a crisp texture that enhances flavor perception.
Cracked wheat has a lower glycemic index than white bread, making it popular in health‑focused diets.
Homemade bread allows control over salt, sugar, and additive levels.
In many cultures toasted bread is served with olive oil, garlic, or spices.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain bread provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and blood‑sugar regulation.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat supplies thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: The bread delivers magnesium, iron, and zinc, important for muscle function and immune health.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Fiber and phytochemicals in whole‑grain bread may help lower cholesterol levels.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: A combination of protein and complex carbohydrates helps maintain fullness longer.

items.title: Wheat allergy / gluten sensitivity
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten intolerance can experience serious reactions to wheat bread.

items.title: Glycemic impact
items.content: Even whole‑grain varieties can raise blood sugar relatively quickly in some individuals.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Store‑bought bakery bread may contain higher sodium than homemade versions.

items.title: Additives
items.content: Commercial breads may include preservatives, emulsifiers, and flavor enhancers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bread can be enjoyed as a snack, spread with butter, avocado, cheese, or used in sandwiches. Toasted slices pair well with soups, salads, and pâtés.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep bread in a paper bag or bread box at room temperature for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag and re‑toast directly from frozen.

content.title: About
content.content: Feta is a traditional Greek cheese made from sheep’s milk, goat’s milk, or a mixture of both. It has a crumbly texture, salty flavor, and a characteristic tangy aroma. Feta is used in salads, pastries, appetizers, and as a standalone table cheese.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Feta holds a Protected Designation of Origin (PDO) status in the EU, meaning only cheese produced in specific Greek regions can be called feta.
Traditionally, feta is aged in a brine of water, salt, and sometimes whey for at least two months.
The cheese is a key ingredient in the classic Greek salad “horiatiki” with olives, tomatoes, and cucumbers.
Ancient Greek texts, including works by Homer, reference cheeses similar to modern feta.
Feta can be made entirely from sheep’s milk, goat’s milk, or a blend, though pure sheep’s milk versions are most common.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Feta provides a high amount of calcium, essential for bone and dental health.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: The cheese supplies high‑quality dairy protein that supports tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains probiotics
items.content: Fermentation introduces beneficial bacteria that may support gut health.

items.title: Lower lactose content
items.content: Fermentation reduces lactose levels, making feta more tolerable for people with mild lactose intolerance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Feta contains vitamin B12, riboflavin, and niacin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Because feta is stored in brine, it can contribute a significant amount of sodium to the diet.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to casein or whey proteins may react to feta.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: While less fatty than many hard cheeses, feta still contains saturated fats, so portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Crumble feta over salads, add it to pastas, casseroles, pizza, or serve with olives and crusty bread. It also works well in marinades and as a stuffing for vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep feta in its original brine in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C, sealed with a lid. If needed, transfer to a fresh brine (water + salt). It lasts 2‑3 weeks. When the brine dries out, the cheese should be dried and consumed within a few days.

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese flavored corn snacks are crunchy bites made from corn dough that are coated with a savory cheese seasoning. They are produced from whole‑grain corn flour, fried or baked until golden, and seasoned with a blend of cheese powder, salt, and spices, giving them a rich, buttery flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: These snacks are often called "corn chips" but differ from traditional potato chips in preparation method.
The cheese flavor comes from real cheese powders and natural flavorings rather than only artificial additives.
Corn‑based snacks are naturally gluten‑free, making them suitable for people with wheat intolerance.
In many markets they are sold in single‑serve packets, ideal for on‑the‑go snacking.
Sodium levels can be high, so checking the nutrition label is recommended.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Corn flour provides a steady release of energy, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Corn is a good source of fiber, which supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Provides vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and supports the nervous system.

items.title: Calcium from cheese seasoning
items.content: The cheese coating can contribute a modest amount of calcium, important for bone health.

items.title: Low in trans fats
items.content: When produced correctly, these snacks can be made without trans fats, making them a safer choice for heart health.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cheese snacks often contain a lot of salt, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Cheese seasonings can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with dairy allergies or lactose intolerance.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: These snacks are energy‑dense, so they should be eaten in moderation, especially when managing weight.

items.title: Additive content
items.content: Some varieties may contain artificial flavors and preservatives that are not suitable for everyone.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cheese flavored corn snacks are convenient to eat straight from the bag as a quick snack. They can be added to salads, used as a crunchy topping for soups, or paired with dips such as guacamole or yogurt‑based sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the snacks in their original sealed bag in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, reseal the bag tightly to keep the crunch. For longer storage, transfer to an airtight container.

content.title: About
content.content: Kung Pao Shrimp is a spicy Chinese dish made with large shrimp, peanuts, vegetables, and a sauce of soy sauce, vinegar, sugar, and dried chili. The dish balances sweet‑spicy flavors, crunchy nuts, and tender seafood.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originates from Sichuan province, famous for its bold, spicy cuisine.
Traditional recipes include fermented black bean sauce, which gives a distinctive aroma.
Peanuts provide not only flavor but also a contrasting crunch.
Shrimp are usually seared until golden and then quickly tossed in the sauce to stay juicy.
Original recipes use dried chili flakes; many restaurants substitute fresh chilies for a brighter heat.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Shrimp supply complete marine protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with many meat dishes, shrimp are low in saturated fats, making them suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Contains omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Omega‑3s support heart health and reduce inflammation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Shrimp are rich in B12 and niacin, important for nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Minerals: zinc and selenium
items.content: These minerals boost immunity and provide antioxidant protection.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Shrimp are a common allergen; individuals with shellfish allergy should avoid this dish.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce and added salt can increase sodium intake, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Spiciness level
items.content: Dried chili makes the dish very hot; those with sensitive stomachs should reduce the amount of chili.

items.title: Potential heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Shrimp harvested from polluted waters may contain cadmium or mercury; choose reputable suppliers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, typically with steamed rice or noodles. Add fresh vegetables such as bell pepper or green onions for brightness. Garnish with extra toasted peanuts and fresh cilantro before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in a skillet or microwave, adding a splash of water to prevent drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Nutrition bar (Zone Perfect Classic Crunch) is a protein bar designed according to the Zone diet principles. It combines slow‑digesting protein, complex carbohydrates and healthy fats to provide steady energy and satiety between meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The bar provides 12 g of protein from whey and soy isolate.
The macronutrient ratio 40 % carbs, 30 % protein, 30 % fat matches Zone diet recommendations.
It contains whole oat, sunflower and toasted rice grains for a crunchy texture.
Each bar delivers 210 kcal, making it a convenient low‑calorie snack.
No artificial colors or flavors are used.

items.title: Supports muscle growth
items.content: High protein content aids muscle repair and growth after training.

items.title: Stabilizes blood sugar
items.content: Balanced carbs‑protein ratio helps prevent rapid glucose spikes.

items.title: Promotes lasting fullness
items.content: Fiber from oats and healthy fats slow gastric emptying.

items.title: Convenient energy source
items.content: Portable and quickly digestible, ideal for an active lifestyle.

items.title: Supports immune function
items.content: B‑vitamins and minerals (magnesium, zinc) contribute to normal immune health.

items.title: Milk or soy allergy
items.content: The bar contains whey protein and soy isolate, which may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Sugar content for low‑carb diets
items.content: Although balanced, the bar includes honey and rice syrup, which may be unsuitable for strict low‑carb regimens.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: At 210 kcal, it is a substantial snack; consider total daily intake when weight‑gaining.

items.title: Fiber load
items.content: High fiber may cause gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the bar straight from the wrapper as a snack between meals, before or after workouts. It can also be sliced and added to yogurt, oatmeal or smoothies to boost protein content.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bars in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, reseal the package tightly or transfer bars to an airtight container to prevent moisture absorption.

content.title: About
content.content: Pancakes are a classic dish made from a thin batter of flour, milk, eggs, and a touch of sugar. The batter cooks quickly on a hot skillet, forming soft, slightly crisp layers. Pancakes are commonly served with sour cream, honey, berries, cottage cheese, or savory fillings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pancakes are known in over 30 countries under different names: crepes (France), blini (Russia), okonomiyaki (Japan).
The tradition of eating pancakes on Maslenitsa in Russia marks the farewell to winter and the arrival of spring.
The world’s largest pancake was made in 2012 in the USA: 15.5 m in diameter and weighing 2.5 t.
Japanese “millet” pancakes are made from rice flour and are gluten‑free.
Pancakes are a frequent contest item because of their versatility and quick preparation.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Pancakes provide a fast‑acting energy source thanks to the carbs in the batter.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs and milk supply a complete set of essential amino acids.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole‑grain flour adds B1, B2 and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus
items.content: Dairy ingredients support bone and tooth health.

items.title: Low fat when lightly cooked
items.content: Using minimal oil keeps pancakes suitable for a balanced diet.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional wheat flour can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Sweet toppings and added sugar increase the calorie load.

items.title: Frying in oil
items.content: Excessive oil adds saturated fat and calories.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Milk in the batter may be problematic for those who cannot digest lactose.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve pancakes hot, rolled or folded. They can be brushed with butter, drizzled with honey, jam, or topped with cottage cheese, or filled with meat, fish, or vegetables. For a lighter version, use whole‑grain or gluten‑free flour.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked pancakes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze them on parchment sheets in bags and reheat in the microwave or skillet.

content.title: About
content.content: Light microwave popcorn is a ready‑to‑eat snack that pops in a few minutes in a microwave oven. It comes in a variety of flavors (cheese, caramel, barbecue, etc.) and has an airy, crunchy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Popcorn is one of the world’s most popular snacks, especially at cinemas.
Microwave popcorn usually contains a small amount of oil and salt, making it less caloric than traditional stovetop popcorn.
Flavorings can be natural (e.g., real cheese) or artificial.
When sealed properly, popcorn stays fresh for up to 12 months.
Light versions have reduced fat and sugar compared with regular popcorn.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Light popcorn provides about 350 kcal per 100 g, making it a suitable snack for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Corn kernels retain most of their dietary fiber, which supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Popcorn is a source of polyphenols that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Corn does not contain gluten, so the product is safe for people with celiac disease.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Popcorn provides thiamine, niacin, and folate, nutrients important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn products.

items.title: Salt and additive content
items.content: Some flavored varieties contain higher levels of salt or artificial sweeteners, which may be undesirable for people with hypertension.

items.title: Overheating risk
items.content: Following the microwave instructions is essential; overheating can cause burning and formation of acrylamide.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Place the bag in the microwave, cook for 2–3 minutes according to the package directions, then let it sit for a minute before opening. Enjoy as a snack, sprinkle over salads, or use as a base for sweet desserts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened bag in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, transfer any remaining popcorn to an airtight container to maintain crunch and flavor.
